If You Bought Alfalfa Sprouting Seed Online This Year, Read This. 
 Two More Alfalfa Recalls Surface the Day After CDC Closed the Seed-Lot Outbreak: Country Creek Acres Alfalfa Sprout Seeds and Francisco Family Foods Alfalfa Sprouts, for E. coli and Salmonella. 77 Sick in 16 States. If You Bought Alfalfa Sprouting Seed Online This Year, Read This.
 By Bill Marler on November 11, 2026 
 Posted in Food Poisoning Information 
 As of November 11, 2026, FDA’s Enforcement Report lists two new recalls tied to the contaminated alfalfa seed lot behind this year’s multistate  E. coli  and  Salmonella  outbreak: Country Creek LLC’s Country Creek Acres Alfalfa Sprout Seeds in 16-ounce packages, and Francisco Family Foods’ hydroponically grown Alfalfa Sprouts in 4-ounce packages, both for possible  E. coli  and  Salmonella  contamination. They appeared November 10, one day after CDC declared the outbreak over at 77 sick in 16 states with six hospitalized and no deaths. Neither recall has an FDA press release, and neither lists lot codes or dates.
 The two recalls are in FDA’s database but have no public notice. 
 Both entries were flagged by Phyllis Entis at  eFoodAlert  on November 10 and link to FDA’s recall database:  Event 100206  for Country Creek LLC and  Event 100236  for Francisco Family Foods. The entries give the product, the package size and the reason, possible  E. coli  and/or  Salmonella  contamination, and for code information say there is none. They do not yet carry a recall initiation date, a quantity, a distribution area or a classification; those fields fill in when FDA publishes the recall in its weekly report, usually two to four weeks after a company starts a recall. Neither company has posted a notice I could find, and FDA has issued no press release for either. If you own either product, you are expected to learn about the recall from a database search.
 These are the seventh and eighth recalls traced to one lot of alfalfa seed. 
 The outbreak began with sprouts. Everything Sprouts LLC of Minnesota recalled its Calco and Everything Sprouts alfalfa sprouts on August 22 and added Robust Radish Sprout Mix on August 28. FDA’s traceback then reached the seed, lot SAL2-24JB, which the still-unnamed seed supplier recalled in late August; FDA’s enforcement report later identified the supplier as International Sprout Holdings of Cookeville, Tennessee. From there the recall walked down the chain to every company that bought from that lot: LEASA Industries sprouts in Florida on September 4, Todd’s Seeds on September 11, Berlin Seeds of Ohio on September 12, and now Country Creek LLC and Francisco Family Foods. Each of those downstream companies sold to home sprouters or to grocers, and each recall reached the public weeks after it started, if it reached the public at all. The seed lot carries a use-by date of December 31, 2029.
 Recall Product Date initiated How the public learned 
 Everything Sprouts Calco and Everything Sprouts alfalfa sprouts; radish mix Aug 28 Aug 22 FDA press release 
 Seed supplier Alfalfa seed lot SAL2-24JB, 43,799 lb Aug 23 Enforcement Report, Sept 10 to 16 
 LEASA Industries Alfalfa sprouts, 4 oz and 6 oz clamshells, FL and NH Sept 4 Enforcement Report, Oct 3 
 Todd’s Seeds Alfalfa seed and five seed mixes, nationwide online Sept 11 Company notice Sept 15 
 Berlin Seeds Alfalfa sprouting seed, 950 lb, 44 states Sept 12 FDA press release Sept 23 
 Country Creek LLC Country Creek Acres Alfalfa Sprout Seeds, 16 oz Not yet posted Enforcement Report, Nov 10 
 Francisco Family Foods Hydroponic alfalfa sprouts, 4 oz Not yet posted Enforcement Report, Nov 10 
 Sources: FDA recall notices, FDA Enforcement Report via openFDA (report dates Sept 10 through Oct 14, 2026), eFoodAlert November 10, 2026; read November 11. Check: seven recalling companies in the table, eight recall actions counting the Everything Sprouts expansion; five reached the public only through the Enforcement Report or a company page. 
 CDC closed the outbreak November 9 at 77 sick in 16 states. 
 CDC’s final update  counts 77 people infected with Shiga toxin-producing  E. coli ,  Salmonella  Agona, or both, in 16 states, with six hospitalized and no deaths. Three people had both infections. Illnesses began May 31 and the last began October 19, nearly two months after the first recall. Minnesota and Wisconsin carried most of the cases. I wrote about  the 76-person count  on October 1, and on Marler Blog about  why the seed problem is not over  even though the outbreak is. The two recalls that surfaced the next morning make the point for me.
 Alfalfa seed keeps for years, which is why these recalls matter after the outbreak is over. 
 A bag of sprouting seed is not a clamshell of sprouts. Sprouts last a week in the refrigerator; seed sits in a pantry for years, and the recalled lot is dated to the end of 2029. Anyone who bought alfalfa sprouting seed online in 2026, from Amazon, a seed company’s website, Etsy, eBay or a garden retailer, should check the brand against the list above. If it is Country Creek Acres, Todd’s Seeds, Berlin Seeds or any alfalfa seed stamped SAL2-24JB, do not sprout it, do not plant it in a kitchen garden you will eat from raw, and do not give it away. Seal it in a bag and throw it out, or contact the seller for a refund. If you have already sprouted seed from one of these brands, throw out the sprouts and wash the jar, lid, screen and tray in hot soapy water or the dishwasher. Sprouting is the problem: warm, wet conditions that make seed germinate also let a few bacteria on a seed coat grow into millions, and no rinse removes them.
 E. coli  and  Salmonella  symptoms start within a week, and children should be watched for kidney trouble. 
 Shiga toxin-producing  E. coli  usually causes severe stomach cramps and diarrhea, often bloody, beginning three to four days after exposure, with little or no fever. Most people recover in a week. About five to ten percent of diagnosed patients, mostly young children and older adults, develop hemolytic uremic syndrome, a form of kidney failure, usually about a week after diarrhea begins; decreased urination, unusual tiredness and pale skin are the warning signs, and they mean the emergency room. Do not take antibiotics or anti-diarrheal medicine for a suspected  E. coli  infection without a doctor’s advice.  Salmonella  Agona causes diarrhea, fever and cramps six hours to six days after exposure and usually resolves in four to seven days. See a doctor for bloody diarrhea, a fever above 102 degrees, vomiting that prevents keeping liquids down, or diarrhea lasting more than three days, and mention raw sprouts or home-sprouted seed.
 Questions people are asking. 
 Is the alfalfa sprout outbreak over? 
 CDC declared it over on November 9, 2026, with 77 sick in 16 states. The outbreak is over because new illnesses stopped being reported, not because the seed is gone. Two more recalls of seed and sprouts from the same lot appeared in FDA’s database on November 10.
 Which alfalfa sprouting seeds have been recalled? 
 Seed lot SAL2-24JB from the supplier, and seed sold under the Todd’s Seeds, Berlin Seeds and Country Creek Acres brands. Todd’s Seeds also recalled five mixes containing alfalfa. Only the Berlin Seeds 5-pound and 50-pound bags and some Todd’s Seeds bags carry a visible lot code; smaller packages often have none, so go by brand and purchase year.
 Can I kill the bacteria by rinsing or soaking the seed? 
 No. Rinsing removes dirt, not bacteria lodged in the seed coat, and soaking in water is the first step of sprouting, which multiplies them. Commercial sprouters treat seed with a strong calcium hypochlorite solution and still have outbreaks. Recalled seed should be discarded.
